question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The place that a person treats as his permanent home, or lives in and has a substantial connection with
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Domicile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Domicile means the place that a person treats as his permanent home, or lives in and has a substantial connection with, even if he is temporarily living elsewhere. (स्थायी निवास स्थान)
◦ Example: Although he works abroad, his domicile remains his ancestral village in Punjab.

• Domicile is a legal as well as everyday term — it denotes the one place a person legally and permanently belongs to, as distinct from a place of merely temporary residence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Oasis (मरूद्यान): A fertile spot in a desert where water is found; also used figuratively for a pleasant place amid unpleasant surroundings.

• Option 3: Embankment (तटबंध): A wall or bank of earth or stone built to prevent a river or the sea from flooding an area.

• Option 4: Resort (सैरगाह): A place frequently visited for relaxation or recreation, such as a holiday destination.

NOTE

• Other commonly asked one-word substitutes on the theme of "home/dwelling": Abode (a place of residence), Habitat (the natural home of an animal or plant), Nomad (a person with no fixed home who moves from place to place), and Migrant (a person who moves from one place to settle in another).

• Do not confuse "Domicile" with "Denizen" (an inhabitant or occupant of a place) — Domicile is the PLACE itself, Denizen is the PERSON living there.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
My friend is owing an expensive cell phone.
option_4: is own an expensive cell phone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. owns an expensive cell phone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Verbs that express a state, possession, or permanent condition (called Stative Verbs) are normally NOT used in the continuous/progressive (-ing) form, even when the action is happening in the present.

• Rule — Stative Verbs of possession: Verbs like own, possess, have (meaning possess), belong describe a state rather than an ongoing action, so they take the Simple Present Tense, not the Present Continuous.
◦ Incorrect: My friend is owning/is owing an expensive cell phone.
◦ Correct: My friend owns an expensive cell phone.

• Since "friend" is third person singular, the simple present verb must take -s/-es: own → owns.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "own an expensive cell phone" is incorrect because it drops the auxiliary/agreement altogether — with a third person singular subject ("My friend"), the simple present verb must be "owns", not the bare form "own".

• Option 3: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original sentence uses the continuous form of a stative verb, which is grammatically wrong and must be corrected.

• Option 4: "is own an expensive cell phone" is incorrect because it is not a valid verb form at all — "is" (an auxiliary) cannot be directly followed by the base form "own" without "-ing" or "to".

NOTE

• Other common stative verbs that avoid the continuous form: know, believe, understand, love, hate, want, need, prefer, seem, appear, belong, contain, consist, resemble.

• Some verbs can be both stative and dynamic depending on meaning — e.g., "think" (stative: "I think he is right"; dynamic: "I am thinking about it"), "have" (stative: "I have a car"; dynamic: "I am having lunch").

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
He has not committed the crime.
option_1: The crime was not committed by him.
option_2: The crime have not being committed by him.
option_3: The crime have not been committed by him.
option_4: The crime has not been committed by him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The crime has not been committed by him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He has not committed the crime" is a negative sentence in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + not + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + not + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the crime" becomes the subject; since it is a singular, third-person subject, the auxiliary used must be "has"; the verb "commit" becomes the past participle "committed"; and "he" becomes the agent as "by him".
◦ Passive: The crime has not been committed by him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was not committed" is the passive of the Simple Past Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "have not being committed" is doubly wrong: it uses the plural auxiliary "have" with the singular subject "the crime", and it wrongly uses "being" instead of the past participle form "been".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it uses "have" instead of "has" — since "the crime" is a singular subject, the auxiliary must agree in number as "has", not "have".

NOTE

• The passive of the Present Perfect Tense always follows the fixed pattern has/have + been + V3; students often confuse "been" (past participle of "be") with "being" (present participle of "be"), which belongs to continuous passive structures instead.

• Subject–verb agreement must always be checked separately from tense: a singular object becoming the new subject in the passive voice takes "has", never "have".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
During the summer of 1893, Miss Sullivan and I visited the World's Fair with Dr. Alexander Graham Bell. I recall with unmixed delight those days when a thousand childish fancies became beautiful realities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. enchant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Delight means great pleasure, joy, or a feeling of being charmed and captivated by something. (अत्यधिक हर्ष/आनंद)
◦ Example: The children squealed with delight when they saw the fireworks.

• Enchant means to fill someone with great delight; to charm or captivate completely, making it the closest match in meaning among the given options — both words describe being filled with intense pleasure or fascination. (मंत्रमुग्ध करना)
◦ Example: The magician's tricks enchanted the entire audience.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: dismay (निराशा): A feeling of concern, disappointment, or distress — this is the OPPOSITE of "delight", not its synonym.

• Option 3: memory (स्मृति): The faculty of recalling past events; it refers to the act of remembering, not to the feeling of pleasure that "delight" conveys.

• Option 4: emotion (भावना): Any strong feeling in general (happiness, anger, sadness, etc.); it is too broad and neutral a word to capture the specifically joyful sense of "delight".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "delight": joy, bliss, rapture, gratification, elation.

• Common antonyms of "delight": dismay, sorrow, displeasure, misery.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Binay said that / he is coming / from / his village, Jaygarh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. he is coming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reports Binay's words using the reporting verb "said", which is in the Past Tense. This is an instance of Narration (Indirect/Reported Speech).

• Rule — Rules of Tense in Narration: When the reporting verb is in the Past Tense, the tense of the reported speech must also shift backward accordingly: Present Continuous ("is coming") changes to Past Continuous ("was coming").
◦ Direct: Binay said, "I am coming from my village, Jaygarh."
◦ Indirect (correct): Binay said that he was coming from his village, Jaygarh.

• Since "said" fixes the reported clause in the past, the segment "he is coming" is grammatically inconsistent and must be "he was coming".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "from" is correctly used as a preposition of origin/direction and contains no error.

• Option 3: "his village, Jaygarh" is grammatically correct — it properly identifies the village by name using an appositive.

• Option 4: "Binay said that" is a correctly formed reporting clause using the conjunction "that" to introduce the noun clause, and contains no error.

NOTE

• Common backward tense shifts in narration: Simple Present → Simple Past; Present Continuous → Past Continuous; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; Simple Past → Past Perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might.

• If the reported statement expresses a universal truth or habitual fact, the tense is NOT changed even when the reporting verb is in the past (e.g., "The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Genial
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Cheerful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Genial means friendly, warm, kind, and pleasant in manner or disposition; having a cheerful and sociable nature. (मिलनसार/प्रसन्नचित्त)
◦ Example: The genial host made all his guests feel welcome and comfortable.

• "Cheerful" best captures the warm, good-humoured friendliness that "genial" describes, whereas the other options relate to hope or positivity rather than warmth of manner.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Optimistic (आशावादी): Hopeful and confident about the future; this describes an outlook on outcomes, not friendliness of manner.

• Option 3: Despondent (निराश): Feeling low-spirited or hopeless — this is nearly the OPPOSITE of "genial".

• Option 4: Positive (सकारात्मक): Constructive or affirmative in attitude; again a matter of outlook rather than warmth or sociability.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "genial": affable, amiable, congenial, cordial, warm-hearted.

• Do not confuse "genial" (friendly) with "genital" or "genius" — a common trap in SSC vocabulary papers due to similar spelling.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. In 1944, he was honoured by King George VI with a Knighthood and became Sir Alexander Fleming.
B. On receiving this great honour, Fleming said in his usual modest way, “Wherever I go, people thank me for saving their lives. I didn't do anything; I just found a remedy that was there.”
C. Fleming became famous overnight and was regarded as one of the most distinguished scientists of his time.
D. The next year, he and his fellow bacteriologists, whose combined efforts had led to the great discovery, were honoured with a joint Nobel Prize.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. CADB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A coherent paragraph must open with the sentence that introduces the main subject/idea, and later sentences must logically build on it using time markers and pronoun/reference links.

• Sentence C is the natural opening line — it introduces the general idea that "Fleming became famous overnight", setting up the topic of the paragraph (his rising fame and honours).

• Sentence A logically follows C by giving the FIRST specific honour in chronological order — "In 1944, he was honoured... with a Knighthood."

• Sentence D follows next with the phrase "The next year", which can only make sense after a year has already been mentioned (1944 in sentence A) — this refers to the joint Nobel Prize, "this great honour" referred to in the following sentence.

• Sentence B concludes the paragraph, referring back to "this great honour" (the Nobel Prize mentioned in D) and giving Fleming's modest reaction to it.

◦ Logical chain: C (general fame) → A (1944 – Knighthood) → D (next year – Nobel Prize) → B (his reaction to "this great honour").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. CADB.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DBCA) is incorrect because it begins with "The next year", which has no prior year reference to link to, and places Fleming's reaction (B) before the fact of his fame is even introduced (C).

• Option 2 (ADBC) is incorrect because it opens directly with the 1944 Knighthood without first establishing the context of Fleming's overnight fame (C), and misplaces the concluding sentence (C) at the end instead of B.

• Option 4 (BCDA) is incorrect because it opens with Fleming's reaction to "this great honour" before that honour (the Nobel Prize) has even been mentioned in the paragraph, making the pronoun reference meaningless.

NOTE

• In para jumble/sentence rearrangement questions, always identify: (1) the sentence that can stand alone as an introduction (no pronouns/references to something not yet mentioned), (2) time-order markers like "the next year", "later", "after this", and (3) pronoun/demonstrative references ("this", "he", "it") that must point back to something already introduced.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Absorbed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Soaked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Absorbed in its primary sense means taken in or soaked up (a liquid, substance, energy, etc.) by chemical or physical action. (सोख लिया गया)
◦ Example: The dry soil quickly absorbed all the rainwater.

• Soaked carries this exact same core meaning of "taken in/drawn in a liquid or substance", making it the most appropriate direct synonym among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Preoccupied (तल्लीन): Means mentally engrossed or lost in thought; this reflects the secondary, figurative sense of "absorbed" (as in "absorbed in a book"), not its primary literal meaning of soaking up a substance.

• Option 3: Restored (पुनर्स्थापित): Means brought back to a former or original condition; it has no meaning connection with "absorbed".

• Option 4: Replaced (प्रतिस्थापित): Means taken the place of something else; this too is unrelated in meaning to "absorbed".

NOTE

• "Absorbed" has two common shades of meaning tested by SSC: (1) literal — soaked up, taken in (a sponge absorbs water); (2) figurative — engrossed, preoccupied (absorbed in a novel). Always check the option set to see which sense is being tested.

• Related word family: absorb (verb), absorption (noun), absorbent (adjective, e.g. "absorbent cotton").

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Allmost.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Almost" — meaning nearly, not quite completely. The word "Allmost" (with a double "l") is incorrect.

• Spelling key: AL + MOST, with only a SINGLE "l". The word is formed from "all" + "most" but drops one "l" when the two are joined into "almost".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Treble" — correctly spelt; means three times as much, or triple.

• Option 2: "Nozzle" — correctly spelt; means a spout fitted to the end of a pipe/hose to control the flow of a liquid or gas.

• Option 4: "Moisture" — correctly spelt; means a small amount of liquid causing dampness.

NOTE

• Other common words that lose a double letter when combined, similar to "almost": already (all + ready), although (all + though), altogether (all + together), welcome (well + come), welfare (well + fare).

• A frequent SSC spelling trap: writing "allmost", "allready", or "allthough" with a double "l" — always remember only a SINGLE "l" is retained after "all" in these compound words.

question: Identify the option that defines the homonyms 'gate' and 'gait' most appropriately.
option_1: Gate means to achieve or receive, and gait means a person's manner of walking.
option_2: Gate means a hinged barrier used to close an opening in a wall, fence or hedge, and gait means a person's manner of walking.
option_3: Gate means general agreement on tariff and excise, and gait means a person's manner of talking.
option_4: Gate means a hinged barrier used to close an opening in a wall or fence, and gait means a cloth or leather leg covering reaching from the instep to above the ankle or to the mid-calf or knee.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Gate means a hinged barrier used to close an opening in a wall, fence or hedge, and gait means a person's manner of walking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Homonyms are words that are pronounced (and sometimes spelt similarly) but have completely different meanings. "Gate" and "gait" are homophones — they sound identical but differ in spelling and meaning.

• Gate means a hinged barrier used to close an opening in a wall, fence, or hedge. (द्वार/फाटक)
◦ Example: Please shut the garden gate after you enter.

• Gait means a person's manner or style of walking. (चाल-ढाल)
◦ Example: The old man had a slow, unsteady gait.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "gate" does not mean "to achieve or receive" — that meaning belongs to a different word, "gain".

• Option 3 is incorrect on both counts: "general agreement on tariff and excise" refers to GATT (an acronym, not "gate"), and "gait" means manner of walking, not manner of talking.

• Option 4 correctly defines "gate" but wrongly defines "gait" as "a cloth or leather leg covering reaching from the instep to above the ankle" — that definition actually belongs to the word "gaiter", not "gait".

NOTE

• Other frequently tested homophone pairs in SSC exams: "bail/bale", "berth/birth", "council/counsel", "principal/principle", "stationary/stationery", "current/currant".

• Memory tip: "gAIT" contains the letter sequence that can be linked to "walkIng" pace — while "gATE" is the simpler, everyday word for a barrier/door.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
She was waiting for a opportunity to start her own business.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. for a opportunity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Use of Articles "a" and "an": The article "a" is used before words that begin with a consonant SOUND, while "an" is used before words that begin with a vowel SOUND (a, e, i, o, u sound), regardless of the actual first letter.

• The word "opportunity" begins with the vowel sound /ɒ/, so it must be preceded by "an", not "a".
◦ Incorrect: for a opportunity
◦ Correct: for an opportunity

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "own business" is grammatically correct — "own" is correctly used as a possessive adjective intensifier before the noun "business".

• Option 2: "to start her" is grammatically correct — it correctly uses the infinitive "to start" followed by the possessive adjective "her".

• Option 4: "She was waiting" is grammatically correct — it correctly uses the Past Continuous Tense (Subject + was/were + V-ing).

NOTE

• Words that sound like they start with a vowel even though their first letter is a consonant also take "an": e.g., an hour, an honest man, an heir, an MBA, an SSC officer (because "h" is silent, or the letter is pronounced as a vowel sound).

• Conversely, words that sound like they start with a consonant even though their first letter is a vowel take "a": e.g., a university, a European, a one-rupee coin, a uniform (because they begin with the /j/ "y" sound).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The players distributed the reward between themselves
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. among themselves.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "Between" vs. "Among": "Between" is used when referring to exactly TWO persons or things, whereas "among" is used when referring to MORE THAN TWO persons or things.

• Since "the players" refers to more than two people, the correct preposition is "among", not "between".

• The correct reflexive pronoun to match the plural subject "the players" is "themselves" (not "their selves" or "their self", which are not valid English words).
◦ Correct: The players distributed the reward among themselves.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "between them" is incorrect because "between" is only appropriate for two people, while "the players" implies more than two.

• Option 3: "between their selves" is incorrect on two counts — it wrongly uses "between" for more than two people, and "their selves" is not a grammatically valid reflexive pronoun (the correct form is "themselves").

• Option 4: "amongst their self" is incorrect because "their self" is not a valid reflexive pronoun; the only correct plural reflexive form is "themselves".

NOTE

• Reflexive pronouns must always agree in number and person with their antecedent: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself (singular); ourselves, yourselves, themselves (plural). "Their self" and "their selves" are common but incorrect forms often used as distractors.

• "Amongst" and "among" are interchangeable in meaning; "amongst" is simply a more formal/older variant, but the pronoun error in Option 4 still makes it incorrect.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. It was the night before the day fixed for his coronation, and the young King was sitting alone in his beautiful chamber.
B. And, indeed, it was the hunters who had found him, coming upon him almost by chance as, bare-limbed and pipe in hand, he was following the flock of the poor goat herd who had brought him up, and whose son he had always fancied himself to be.
C. The lad—for he was only a lad, being but sixteen years of age—was not sorry at their departure, and had flung himself back with a deep sigh of relief on the soft cushions of his embroidered couch, lying there, wild-eyed and open-mouthed, like a brown woodland Faun, or some young animal of the forest newly snared by the hunters.
D. His courtiers had all taken their leave of him, bowing their heads to the ground, according to the ceremonious usage of the day, and had retired to the Great Hall of the Palace, to receive a few last lessons from the Professor of Etiquette; there being some of them who had still quite natural manners, which in a courtier is, I need hardly say, a very grave offence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. ADCB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A well-arranged paragraph must begin with a sentence that sets the scene without depending on any earlier reference, and each subsequent sentence should connect to the one before it through pronouns, articles, or logical continuity.

• Sentence A is the ideal opening line — it independently sets the scene: "It was the night before the day fixed for his coronation, and the young King was sitting alone in his beautiful chamber."

• Sentence D logically follows A, explaining WHY the King is alone — "His courtiers had all taken their leave of him... and had retired to the Great Hall."

• Sentence C follows D, referring back to the courtiers' exit with the phrase "was not sorry at their departure" — "their" clearly refers to the courtiers mentioned in D.

• Sentence B concludes the paragraph, beginning with "And, indeed, it was the hunters who had found him", which picks up the simile in C ("newly snared by the hunters") and extends it into the narrative about the hunters and the goatherd who raised him.

◦ Logical chain: A (scene set) → D (courtiers leave) → C (King reacts, not sorry at their departure) → B (backstory of the hunters/goatherd).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. ADCB.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (CBDA) is incorrect because it opens with "The lad... was not sorry at their departure" before "their" (the courtiers) has even been introduced, and ends with A, which must logically come first as the scene-setting sentence.

• Option 3 (ACDB) is incorrect because it places D between C and B; but D (courtiers taking leave) must come immediately after A and before C, since C's "their departure" specifically refers to the courtiers' leave-taking described in D.

• Option 4 (CDBA) is incorrect because it begins with "the lad... was not sorry at their departure" before any departure (D) or scene (A) has been established, making the pronoun reference meaningless at the start.

NOTE

• In descriptive/narrative paragraph jumbles, look first for the sentence that can stand independently as scene-setting (often containing "It was...", proper nouns, or a clear time/place marker) — this is almost always the opening sentence.

• Track pronoun chains carefully ("their", "him", "he") — a sentence using a pronoun cannot precede the sentence that first introduces its antecedent.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains a spelling error.
If more is desired than the instantanious impact on the mind, the advertising value of the poster falls sharply, within limits of outdoor publicity, however it is at present unchallenged.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. instantanious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "instantaneous" — meaning occurring or done immediately, without any perceptible delay. The given form "instantanious" is misspelt.

• Spelling key: INSTANT + ANEOUS. Note the ending is "-aneous" (as in "spontaneous", "simultaneous", "extraneous"), not "-anious".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "unchallenged" — correctly spelt; means not disputed or opposed.

• Option 3: "desired" — correctly spelt; past tense/participle of "desire", meaning wished for or wanted.

• Option 4: "advertising" — correctly spelt; the present participle/gerund of "advertise".

NOTE

• Words ending in the "-aneous" sound are a common spelling trap in SSC papers: simultaneous, spontaneous, extraneous, miscellaneous, instantaneous — all end in "-aneous", never "-anious".

• Remember the root connection: "instantaneous" is built on "instant" + the suffix "-aneous", which helps recall the correct ending.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Wedding invitations will be sent by them.
option_1: They will be sent wedding invitations.
option_4: He will be send wedding invitations.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They will send wedding invitations.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Wedding invitations will be sent by them" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Future Tense.

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + will be + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + will + V1 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "by them" becomes the subject "They"; the auxiliary "will" is retained; the past participle "sent" reverts to its base form "send"; and "wedding invitations" becomes the object.
◦ Active: They will send wedding invitations.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "They will be sent wedding invitations" is incorrect because it retains the passive structure ("will be sent") instead of converting it into an active verb form.

• Option 2: "He will sent wedding invitations" is incorrect both in subject (it wrongly changes "they" to "he") and in verb form (the base form after "will" must be "send", not the past form "sent").

• Option 4: "He will be send wedding invitations" is incorrect because it wrongly changes the subject to "He", and "will be send" is not a valid active-voice verb structure.

NOTE

• When converting passive to active in the Simple Future Tense, always restore the verb to its base/first form (V1) after "will" — never keep the past participle (V3) that was used in the passive structure.

• The subject of the active sentence must exactly match the agent named after "by" in the passive sentence — do not change "them" to "he" or any other pronoun.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Her room looks very messy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Organised.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Messy means untidy, dirty, or disorganised; not arranged neatly. (अस्त-व्यस्त)
◦ Example: His desk was messy, with papers scattered everywhere.

• Organised means arranged in a neat, orderly, and systematic manner — the exact opposite of "messy". (व्यवस्थित)
◦ Example: Her organised study table made it easy to find any book quickly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Untidy (अस्त-व्यस्त): Means not neat or orderly — this is a SYNONYM of "messy", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Chaotic (अराजक): Means in a state of complete disorder and confusion — again a SYNONYM of "messy".

• Option 3: Disordered (अव्यवस्थित): Means lacking order or organisation — this too is a SYNONYM of "messy", not an antonym.

NOTE

• A common trap in antonym questions is including several synonyms of the given word among the options, with only one genuine antonym — always check each option's own meaning carefully rather than picking the first "different-sounding" word.

• Other antonyms of "messy": neat, tidy, orderly, systematic, spick-and-span.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A perfect storm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The worst possible situation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A perfect storm" means a particularly bad or critical situation caused by a rare combination of unfavourable circumstances occurring together; the worst possible situation. (सबसे बुरी स्थिति)
◦ Example: Rising fuel prices, a labour shortage, and falling demand created a perfect storm for the airline industry.

• The expression comes from meteorology, where a "perfect storm" refers to a storm of maximum intensity created by a rare, simultaneous combination of adverse weather conditions — figuratively extended to describe any disastrous convergence of negative factors.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To have pretty good judgement (अच्छा निर्णय लेना): This describes sound decision-making, unrelated to the idiom "a perfect storm".

• Option 2: Healing from trauma (आघात से उबरना): This describes recovery from a difficult past experience, not the meaning of the given idiom.

• Option 4: Appropriate for all occasions (हर अवसर के लिए उपयुक्त): This describes versatility or suitability, which is unrelated to and almost opposite in tone to "a perfect storm".

NOTE

• Other idioms describing bad/critical situations often asked in SSC: "Between the devil and the deep sea" (caught between two equally unpleasant choices), "Out of the frying pan into the fire" (moving from a bad situation to a worse one), and "A Pandora's box" (a source of many unforeseen troubles).

question:
Select the sentence that has the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Bad blood
option_1: She is so scared of cockroaches that she fainted when she saw them crawling near her foot.
option_2: The doctor dropped the bad news to Ravi as he was suffering from a serious disease.
option_3: The gangster had some bitter relations with a local activist so he warned him to stay out of his business.
option_4: Sushant always gets in trouble for telling lies but he never learns anything.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The gangster had some bitter relations with a local activist so he warned him to stay out of his business.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bad blood" means long-standing feelings of hostility, resentment, or animosity between people. (आपसी शत्रुता/कटुता)
◦ Example: There has been bad blood between the two families ever since the property dispute.

• In Option 3, the phrase "bitter relations" between the gangster and the local activist, leading to a warning, is a direct real-life illustration of ongoing hostility — exactly matching the sense of "bad blood".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 illustrates the idiom "to have cold feet" or a simple fear of insects, not hostility between people — unrelated to "bad blood".

• Option 2 illustrates breaking bad news gently, not a relationship of hostility — unrelated to "bad blood".

• Option 4 illustrates a person's habitual lying and failure to learn from mistakes, which relates to idioms like "a leopard cannot change its spots", not to "bad blood".

NOTE

• Other idioms of conflict/hostility commonly tested by SSC: "To bear a grudge" (to feel resentment towards someone), "At daggers drawn" (in a state of intense hostility), and "To rub someone the wrong way" (to irritate or annoy someone).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
After my first visit to Boston, I spent almost every winter in the North. Once I went on a visit to a New England village with its frozen lakes and vast snow fields.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. extensive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Vast means very great in size, extent, or amount; extremely large. (विशाल)
◦ Example: The vast desert stretched as far as the eye could see.

• Extensive means covering or affecting a large area; very great in size or extent, making it the closest synonym to "vast" among the given options. (विस्तृत)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: minimal (न्यूनतम): Means the smallest possible amount or degree — this is nearly the OPPOSITE of "vast".

• Option 2: shallow (उथला): Means having little depth; it describes depth, not size or extent, and is unrelated to "vast".

• Option 4: solid (ठोस): Means firm and stable in shape, or made of consistent material throughout; it describes physical density/state, not size or extent.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "vast": immense, enormous, huge, colossal, expansive, boundless.

• Common antonyms of "vast": tiny, minute, minimal, limited, narrow.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Hardly we had boarded the train when it started to move.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had we boarded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Inversion with "Hardly...when" / "No sooner...than": When a sentence begins with the negative adverb "Hardly" (or "Scarcely", "No sooner"), the normal subject-verb order is INVERTED — the auxiliary verb must come BEFORE the subject.

• Structure: Hardly + had + Subject + V3 + when + Subject + V2 (Past Simple)...
◦ Incorrect: Hardly we had boarded the train when it started to move.
◦ Correct: Hardly had we boarded the train when it started to move.

• This inversion is used to describe two actions occurring in quick succession — the boarding of the train happens just before it starts moving, expressed using the Past Perfect Tense in the "Hardly" clause.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "will we boarded" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes the future auxiliary "will" with the past form "boarded", and does not follow the "Hardly + had + Subject + V3" inversion structure.

• Option 2: "we are boarded" is incorrect because it fails to invert the subject and auxiliary, and uses the present tense "are", which does not fit the past narrative context.

• Option 3: "is we boarded" is incorrect because "is" cannot combine grammatically with the plural subject "we", and this is not a valid verb structure at all.

NOTE

• Other negative adverbials that trigger subject-auxiliary inversion when placed at the start of a sentence: Never, Rarely, Seldom, Little, Not only, No sooner, Under no circumstances, On no account.
◦ Example: "No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out."
◦ Example: "Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The basic elements of computers that (1)_________ our world are explained in an interactive manner. The book has a (2)_________ approach of colourful and creative picture-based activities. The puzzles, activities and mazes (3)_________ the students to develop critical thinking, logical and motor skills. After every lesson, (4)_________ exercises are incorporated to (5)_________ the conceptual understanding of the students.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. empower.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in the relative clause **"the basic elements of computers that (1)___ our world". The relative pronoun "that" refers back to its antecedent "elements"**, which is PLURAL.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement in relative clauses: The verb inside a relative clause introduced by "that"/"which"/"who" must agree in number with the antecedent noun the relative pronoun stands for, not with any other noun nearby.

• Since "elements" is plural, the verb must also be plural: empower (base form used for plural subjects in the Simple Present Tense).

• Meaning-wise, "empower" means to give someone the ability or power to do something, which fits perfectly with computers enabling/enhancing our world.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "negate" is incorrect in meaning — "negate" means to cancel out or make ineffective, which contradicts the positive tone of the passage describing how computer elements benefit our world.

• Option 3: "empowers" is grammatically incorrect — the singular form "empowers" does not agree with the plural antecedent "elements".

• Option 4: "negates" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 (wrong meaning) and would also require checking agreement, but is ruled out primarily on meaning grounds.

NOTE

• When a relative clause comes between a plural head noun and its verb (e.g., "elements of computers that ___"), always trace the verb's agreement back to the head noun ("elements"), not to the noun closest to the blank ("computers").

• "Empower" collocates commonly with technology-related passages in SSC comprehension/cloze questions: "empower users", "empower students", "empower communities".

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The basic elements of computers that (1)_________ our world are explained in an interactive manner. The book has a (2)_________ approach of colourful and creative picture-based activities. The puzzles, activities and mazes (3)_________ the students to develop critical thinking, logical and motor skills. After every lesson, (4)_________ exercises are incorporated to (5)_________ the conceptual understanding of the students.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. unique.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"The book has a (2)___ approach of colourful and creative picture-based activities."** The tone of the sentence is clearly positive, praising the book's method of teaching through colourful, creative activities.

• "Unique" means being the only one of its kind; distinctive and special, which fits naturally with a book being praised for its special, creative teaching approach.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "difficult" does not fit — a "difficult approach" carries a negative connotation, which clashes with the positive description ("colourful and creative") in the sentence.

• Option 2: "complex" does not fit for the same reason — a "complex approach" suggests complication, which does not match the light, engaging tone of "colourful and creative picture-based activities".

• Option 3: "trivial" does not fit because it means unimportant or insignificant, which would undermine rather than praise the book's approach.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always match the connotation (positive/negative) of the missing word to the surrounding descriptive words — here, "colourful and creative" signals that a positive, complimentary adjective like "unique" is required.

• Common collocations: "a unique approach", "a unique perspective", "a unique style" are frequently used in descriptive/review-style passages.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The basic elements of computers that (1)_________ our world are explained in an interactive manner. The book has a (2)_________ approach of colourful and creative picture-based activities. The puzzles, activities and mazes (3)_________ the students to develop critical thinking, logical and motor skills. After every lesson, (4)_________ exercises are incorporated to (5)_________ the conceptual understanding of the students.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. help.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"The puzzles, activities and mazes (3)___ the students to develop critical thinking, logical and motor skills." The subject here is a compound subject — "puzzles, activities and mazes"** — joined by "and", making it PLURAL.

• Rule — Compound Subjects joined by "and": When two or more subjects are joined by "and", the verb used with them must be PLURAL.

• The rest of the passage is written in the Simple Present Tense ("are explained", "has", "are incorporated"), so the blank must also take the plural, simple present form: help.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "helped" is incorrect because it is in the Past Tense, which breaks the Simple Present Tense used consistently throughout the passage.

• Option 3: "helps" is incorrect because it is the singular form of the verb, which does not agree with the plural compound subject "puzzles, activities and mazes".

• Option 4: "had helped" is incorrect because it is in the Past Perfect Tense, which does not match the present-tense, general-description style of the rest of the passage.

NOTE

• Compound subjects joined by "and" almost always take a plural verb (e.g., "Rice and beans are served together"), except when the two nouns together refer to a single unit or concept (e.g., "Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast").

• Always scan a cloze passage for its overall tense pattern before filling in a blank — consistency with surrounding verbs ("are explained", "are incorporated") is a strong clue to the correct tense.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The basic elements of computers that (1)_________ our world are explained in an interactive manner. The book has a (2)_________ approach of colourful and creative picture-based activities. The puzzles, activities and mazes (3)_________ the students to develop critical thinking, logical and motor skills. After every lesson, (4)_________ exercises are incorporated to (5)_________ the conceptual understanding of the students.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. brainstorming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"After every lesson, (4)___ exercises are incorporated to (5)___ the conceptual understanding of the students."** The purpose stated is to strengthen the students' understanding, so the missing adjective must describe a positive, thought-provoking kind of exercise.

• "Brainstorming" means a method of encouraging creative thinking and generating ideas through active mental engagement, making "brainstorming exercises" a natural, positive collocation that fits the goal of deepening conceptual understanding.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "superficial" does not fit — it means shallow or lacking depth, which contradicts the stated purpose of strengthening "conceptual understanding".

• Option 3: "baffling" does not fit — it means confusing or puzzling in a negative sense, which would hinder rather than help understanding.

• Option 4: "irrational" does not fit — it means not logical or sensible, which is inconsistent with an educational exercise meant to build critical thinking.

NOTE

• "Brainstorming" is a well-known collocation in educational and business contexts: "brainstorming session", "brainstorming exercise", "brainstorming activity" — all describing structured idea-generation or reflective practice.

• When filling blanks describing educational tools/exercises, always favour words with a constructive, positive connotation that supports the stated learning goal.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The basic elements of computers that (1)_________ our world are explained in an interactive manner. The book has a (2)_________ approach of colourful and creative picture-based activities. The puzzles, activities and mazes (3)_________ the students to develop critical thinking, logical and motor skills. After every lesson, (4)_________ exercises are incorporated to (5)_________ the conceptual understanding of the students.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. evolve.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"...exercises are incorporated to (5)___ the conceptual understanding of the students." The blank directly follows the infinitive marker "to"**.

• Rule — Infinitive of Purpose: When "to" is used to express purpose (answering "why"), it must be followed by the BASE FORM (V1) of the verb — this structure is called the "infinitive of purpose".
◦ Structure: to + V1 (base form)

• Since the sentence expresses the purpose of the exercises (i.e., "in order to develop/strengthen understanding"), the base verb form "evolve" must follow "to".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "evolving" is incorrect because the -ing form cannot directly follow the infinitive marker "to" in a purpose construction.

• Option 2: "evolved" is incorrect because the past tense/participle form cannot follow "to" in this structure.

• Option 3: "evolution" is incorrect because it is a noun, not a verb, and grammatically cannot follow "to" in an infinitive-of-purpose structure that requires a verb.

NOTE

• The infinitive of purpose ("to + V1") is extremely common in SSC grammar and cloze questions: "to improve", "to develop", "to strengthen", "to enhance" — always the bare base form.

• Do not confuse the infinitive marker "to" (followed by a base verb) with "to" used as a preposition (followed by a noun/gerund, e.g., "look forward to seeing you").
